items.title: Preserve validation errors for invalid TUI keybindings
items.body:
Preserve validation errors for invalid TUI keybindings

## Why

Deserializing keybindings through an untagged enum hides the specific validation error, making invalid `tui.keymap` settings harder to diagnose.

## What changed

Deserialize single keybinding strings and lists by value type so validation errors reach the user. Errors now retain the reason a binding is invalid and the affected configuration key, including when loading configuration for `codex mcp list`.

## Testing

Add TOML regression tests for unknown keys, invalid chord strokes, and overly long chords in both string and list forms. Add a CLI snapshot test verifying that `codex mcp list` reports the invalid keybinding reason and configuration key.

items.title: macOS: restricted-network SSH failure surfaces as DNS error (-65563) without clear policy/recovery diagnostics

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
## Summary
On macOS, agent-executed Git/SSH queries failed with a DNS-looking error while the identical read-only command worked in the user's normal Terminal. After the session changed to a network-enabled execution profile, the agent could run the same query successfully. Please improve diagnostics so users can distinguish an execution-policy denial from an actual DNS/server problem without weakening sandbox protections.

## Environment
- Platform: macOS.
- Surface: a Codex session executing local shell commands.
- Exact app/CLI versions were not captured; no version is inferred from another installed binary.
- Subscription and private session identifiers are intentionally omitted.

## Observed sequence
1. A Git push to an SSH remote succeeded and returned a successful remote ref update.
2. A subsequent agent-executed read-only query failed:

```sh
git ls-remote ssh://git@<redacted-host>:2222/<redacted-owner>/<redacted-repository>.git refs/heads/master
```

```text
ssh: Could not resolve hostname <redacted-host>: -65563
fatal: Could not read from remote repository.
```

3. A second agent execution reproduced the same error. A Python socket probe could create an AF_INET socket, but getaddrinfo for that host failed with errno 8: nodename nor servname provided, or not known. A target-specific dscacheutil lookup returned no records.
4. The user ran the identical Git query in normal Terminal on the same Mac. It succeeded and returned the expected master ref.
5. An agent-executed GitHub CLI query also reported error connecting to api.github.com.
6. After the session execution profile changed to network-enabled, without this agent changing DNS, SSH, remote-server or project settings, both the original Git query and the GitHub CLI query succeeded.

The hostname, owner, repository, commit hash, local paths, account details and credentials have been redacted. The placeholder command describes the observed case; it is not a standalone reproduction against a supplied public host.

## Expected behavior
- When networking is prohibited by the execution profile, explain the effective restriction clearly instead of leaving only a misleading DNS-style error.
- Distinguish policy-denied/unavailable-network execution from a genuine DNS failure when the execution layer has enough information.
- Give accurate, supported guidance for changing an authorized execution profile or handing off the query; do not suggest rebooting the user's Mac or changing a working remote service.
- If permissions change between commands or turns, make the effective state clear enough to explain why a previous push worked while a later query did not.

## Scope and uncertainty
This is a diagnostics/usability report, not proof of a defective DNS implementation or a request to bypass security. The underlying denial mechanism and reason for the initial successful push were not independently established. Recovery correlates with the execution-profile change; versions, detailed policy rules and private logs were not collected.

Related closed report: #12867 describes Linux sandbox DNS/socket failures. This report adds the macOS -65563 observation, same-machine Terminal comparison and successful read-only queries after a profile change.

## Impact
The agent could not verify a completed push or continue CI status checks, requiring the user to repeat commands manually and causing confusion about whether their machine or Git server needed repair. No private transcripts or logs are attached.

items.title: Code Mode: list already-completed tool calls when an exec script fails

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI

### What feature would you like to see?

#### Summary

When a Code Mode script throws partway through, include the nested tool calls that already ran (name and status) in the error the model sees, so it does not repeat side effects when it retries.

#### Problem to solve

A failing `exec` returns any partial output plus `Script error:` and the stack (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/code_mode/mod.rs`, `codex-rs/code-mode-runtime/src/runtime/value.rs`). Nested calls that already finished are not rolled back, but the error does not say which ones ran. A script that creates tickets, posts comments, or writes files in a loop and then throws on item 7 leaves the model unsure whether items 1–6 happened, and the natural retry re-runs the whole script and duplicates them.

#### Proposed behavior

- On script failure (exception, termination, or timeout), the result includes a short summary of nested tool calls made before the failure, each with its tool name and outcome (completed, failed, cancelled), and a note that completed calls were not undone.
- On success, output is unchanged.
- The summary is bounded so a script with thousands of calls cannot flood the result.

#### Acceptance criteria

- A script that calls a write-capable tool three times and then throws returns an error whose text names those three calls as completed and states they were not undone.
- A script that throws before any tool call says that no tool calls were made.
- A script terminated with `wait` and `terminate: true` reports calls that were still running as cancelled.
- The summary stays within a fixed size and notes how many calls were omitted.

#### Affected area

Code Mode error formatting (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/code_mode`).

#### Non-goals

- Rolling back side effects.
- Changing the metadata recorded by the `executed_tool_call_metadata` feature, which is request metadata rather than text the model reads.

### Additional information

- Variant: CLI. Checked against `openai/codex` main at `da2e174a66` and `codex-cli 0.159.3`.
- Prior art: Pi's codemode appends "Tool calls made before the failure (they are not undone): name (status), …" to the stack trace (`earendil-works/pi`, `packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/codemode/execute.ts`).

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI

### What feature would you like to see?

#### Summary

When an `exec` result is cut to fit `max_output_tokens`, save the complete output to a file and tell the model the path, so it can read the dropped middle instead of re-running the script.

#### Problem to solve

Code Mode truncates long script output by keeping the head and tail (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/code_mode/mod.rs`, `codex-rs/utils/output-truncation`). The dropped middle is gone. If the needed rows were in the middle, the model has to re-run the script, repeating every nested tool call, including calls with side effects or rate limits, or guess.

#### Proposed behavior

- When truncation happens, the full text output of the cell is written to a file Codex manages for the session.
- The truncated result ends with a line naming that path and how to read it (for example with offset/limit), or says why saving failed.
- Untruncated results are unchanged.

#### Acceptance criteria

- A script that emits 5,000 numbered lines with `max_output_tokens` set to 500 returns a truncated result whose last line gives a file path; reading that file shows all 5,000 lines in order.
- The model can read the file with its normal file-reading tool under the default sandbox and approval settings.
- When the file cannot be written, the result says so and still returns the truncated text.
- Scripts whose output fits the budget produce no file and no extra line.

#### Affected area

Code Mode output handling (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/code_mode`), session temp storage.

#### Non-goals

- Changing the default output budget or truncation strategy.
- Saving image or audio items.

### Additional information

- Variant: CLI. Checked against `openai/codex` main at `da2e174a66` and `codex-cli 0.159.3`.
- Related: #42367 (no upper bound on `max_output_tokens` in Code Mode). This request is about not losing data when truncation does happen.
- Prior art: Pi's codemode writes the full output to a temp file and appends `[Full output: <path> (read with offset/limit)]` to the truncated result (`earendil-works/pi`, `packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/codemode/execute.ts`).

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI

### What feature would you like to see?

#### Summary

Give Code Mode scripts a helper that sends a short prompt to a configured (cheap) model and returns its answer, so a script can triage many tool results without routing them all back through the main model.

#### Problem to solve

A common Code Mode job is "fetch 200 issues/emails/log lines over MCP, then decide which ones matter". Scripts can fetch and filter with plain JavaScript, but anything needing judgment (sentiment, relevance, category) has to be returned to the main model as raw text. That spends the main model's context and tokens on exactly the bulk data Code Mode is meant to keep out of the transcript. The script helpers today are `exit`, `text`, `image`, `audio`, `generatedImage`, `store`, `load`, `notify`, `setTimeout`/`clearTimeout`, `ALL_TOOLS`, and `yield_control` (`codex-rs/code-mode-protocol/src/description.rs`); none calls a model.

#### Proposed behavior

- A script-level helper (for example `models.classify(...)` or `models.complete(...)`) sends a prompt plus input to a model chosen by config, and resolves to the model's text or a label from a given set.
- The model used is chosen by the user's config (for example a "classifier model" setting), never by script-supplied endpoints or credentials.
- Calls appear as nested calls in the transcript UI and count toward session usage.
- Concurrency is capped so `Promise.all` over hundreds of items cannot flood the provider.
- The `exec` description documents the helper, its model selection, and its limits.

#### Acceptance criteria

- A script that runs the helper over 50 strings with labels `["positive","negative","neutral"]` returns one valid label per string, and only the script's summarized output reaches the main model.
- The helper uses the configured model; a script cannot pass a base URL, API key, or headers that receive the user's credentials.
- Token usage from these calls shows up in the session's usage totals.
- With no classifier model configured, the helper rejects with a clear error and the script can catch it.

#### Affected area

Code Mode script API and description (`codex-rs/code-mode-protocol`, `codex-rs/core/src/tools/code_mode`), model configuration, usage accounting.

#### Non-goals

- Full sub-agent spawning from scripts.
- Letting scripts pick arbitrary providers or endpoints.

#### Alternatives considered

- Exposing an MCP server that wraps a model: works today but puts credentials and model choice outside Codex's config and usage tracking.

### Additional information

- Variant: CLI. Checked against `openai/codex` main at `da2e174a66` and `codex-cli 0.159.3`; searching all branches found no model-call helper for Code Mode.
- Prior art: Pi's codemode exposes `models.getModelOfType()` and `models.classify()` to scripts, re-resolves the model by provider and id so script-supplied headers never receive credentials, and caps classify concurrency at 4 (`earendil-works/pi`, `packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/codemode/execute.ts`, `tool.ts`).

items.title: Code Mode: persist store/load values across session resume and fork

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI

### What feature would you like to see?

#### Summary

Values a Code Mode script saves with `store()` should still be there after `codex resume` or a fork, scoped to the conversation branch that wrote them.

#### Problem to solve

`store()`/`load()` exist so later `exec` calls can reuse state such as a fetched issue list, a cursor, or an index built from a large MCP result. Today that state lives only in the runtime's memory (`stored_values: Mutex<HashMap<…>>` in `codex-rs/code-mode-runtime/src/session_runtime/mod.rs`), so it disappears when the session is resumed, the app restarts, or the conversation is forked. The model's transcript still says "I stored X under key Y", but `load("Y")` now returns `undefined` and the script has to redo the expensive tool calls.

#### Proposed behavior

- Values written by `store()` in a successful `exec` are recorded with the session, so `load()` returns them after resume.
- On fork, the new branch sees the values stored up to the fork point; later writes on either branch do not leak into the other.
- A failed script's writes follow one documented rule (kept or discarded).
- `store(key, undefined)` removes the key instead of throwing.

#### Acceptance criteria

- In a session, an `exec` runs `store("k", {n: 1})`; after quitting and running `codex resume` on that session, an `exec` running `text(JSON.stringify(load("k")))` prints `{"n":1}`.
- After forking at a point where `k` = 1 and then storing `k` = 2 on the original branch, `load("k")` on the fork returns 1.
- `store("k", undefined)` succeeds and a later `load("k")` returns `undefined`.
- Size limits for persisted values are documented in the `exec` tool description.

#### Affected area

Code Mode runtime (`codex-rs/code-mode-runtime`), session persistence and resume/fork.

#### Non-goals

- Sharing stored values across different sessions or projects.
- Persisting values from cells that were terminated mid-run.

### Additional information

- Variant: CLI. Checked against `openai/codex` main at `da2e174a66` and `codex-cli 0.159.3`.
- Several bundled models use `"tool_mode": "code_mode_only"` in `codex-rs/models-manager/models.json`, so `exec` is the only way those models reach tools and this state matters for normal use.
- Prior art: Pi's codemode (`earendil-works/pi`, `packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/codemode/execute.ts`) records successful `store()` writes as session entries and replays them along the current branch, so values survive resume and stay branch-scoped.

items.body:
Title: Desktop sidebar: cannot unpin remote threads while their host is offline

Environment
- Codex desktop app on macOS; remote Windows host currently offline, as reported by the user.
- App version not captured.
- Reproduced on two pinned remote threads using the Codex app tools connector.

Steps to reproduce
1. Pin a chat associated with a remote host.
2. Leave the remote host offline.
3. Call list_threads: the pinned chat remains present, but title, hostId, cwd and other metadata are null.
4. Call move_thread_to_sidebar_section with the listed threadId, hostId="local" (the local sidebar), and sectionId=null to remove it from Pinned.

Actual behavior
Both operations return isError=true with:
"Could not determine whether Codex thread <thread-id> exists. Unavailable or failed hosts: <remote-host-id>"
The two entries remain pinned. No manual UI unpin attempt was made; this reproduction is specifically through the app tools connector.

Expected behavior
Removing a saved sidebar pin should work locally even when the remote host is offline. The local sidebar already retains the thread identity and pin order, and updating this preference should not require fetching the remote transcript or confirming the remote thread still exists.

Impact
Users cannot clean up stale remote pins through the connector unless they reconnect a machine that may rarely or never be powered on. Missing cached titles also makes these entries hard to identify.

Suggested direction (hypothesis, not source-code diagnosis)
Resolve sidebar removal from the locally persisted item identity before attempting remote thread existence lookup. Retain cached display metadata or show a clear offline label.

Privacy
Thread IDs, host IDs, chat contents, credentials and session logs omitted.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.928.31416

### What subscription do you have?

plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

Conversation messages are not persisted in an SMB/UNC workspace and disappear after restarting Codex.

I am using Codex on native Windows, without WSL. The project is accessed through a Samba network share:

\\<SERVER>\<SHARE>\

This same workspace previously saved conversations successfully. Now, user messages and assistant replies are visible while the app is open, but after exiting and reopening Codex, the thread remains in the sidebar while its conversation content is empty.

Conversations created in a normal local directory save successfully.

The local logs repeatedly show the following errors:

failed to record rollout items: thread-store internal error: permission path cannot be represented losslessly

failed to flush rollout writer; reopening and retrying: permission path cannot be represented losslessly

retrying rollout writer flush failed; first error: permission path cannot be represented losslessly; final error: permission path cannot be represented losslessly

Read-only inspection found that an affected new thread has zero rows in the thread_items table of thread_history_1.sqlite. Its rollout file contains setup/context records but no assistant replies.

Existing UNC conversations also started failing to persist new messages, while their previously saved content is still present.

Regression timeline (UTC+8):
- The same workspace saved replies successfully with runtime 0.155.0-alpha.9.2 and 0.155.0-alpha.16.
- Another UNC workspace saved replies with 0.155.0-alpha.16.3 on September 28, 2026.
- On September 29 at 09:44:27, the app startup log reports runtime 0.158.0-alpha.2.1.
- The earliest retained occurrence of the persistence error is September 29 at 09:48:22.
- The problem persists with runtime 0.159.0 and 0.159.2.

Older working threads and newer failing threads have the same database cwd representation:

\\?\UNC\<SERVER>\<SHARE>

Current Codex app version: 26.928.31416
Current bundled runtime: 0.159.2

Potentially related issue:
https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48443

That issue reports the same permission-path error with runtime 0.158.0-alpha.2.1, but concerns tool execution under Windows/WSL. My issue concerns conversation persistence on native Windows with an SMB/UNC workspace.

The evidence suggests a regression in permission-path serialization or conversation persistence, but the exact cause has not been confirmed.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. On native Windows, open an SMB/Samba UNC directory as a project in Codex, for example:

   \\<SERVER>\<SHARE>\

2. Create a new conversation in that project.

3. Send a simple prompt such as:

   Hello. Please reply with "UNC_HISTORY_TEST_OK".

4. Wait until the assistant finishes replying and the turn is complete.

5. Exit Codex normally.

6. Reopen Codex and select the same conversation from the project sidebar.

Expected:
The user prompt and completed assistant reply are still visible.

Actual:
The conversation remains listed in the sidebar, but its message content is empty.

Control test:
Repeat the same steps with a project in a normal local Windows directory. In my testing, the local-directory conversation is preserved after restarting Codex.

Additional observations:
- The UNC workspace previously saved conversations successfully.
- Existing UNC conversations also started failing to save new messages.
- Logs report:
  failed to record rollout items: thread-store internal error: permission path cannot be represented losslessly
- The affected new thread has zero rows in thread_history_1.sqlite's thread_items table.

Affected thread/session ID:
01a0f5e0-abba-76a3-a735-921af34bf3c9

Token limit usage / context window usage:
Not recorded. The issue also occurs with a short greeting conversation and does not require a long context or substantial token usage.

No code snippet is required to reproduce this issue; it occurs during normal conversation persistence.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should persist user messages and assistant replies for conversations in SMB/UNC workspaces, as it previously did.

After a completed turn, exiting and reopening the app should preserve the full conversation. Selecting the thread from the sidebar should display all previously saved messages, and existing threads should continue saving new messages.

If a persistence error occurs, the app should clearly warn the user that the conversation has not been saved, so they can copy or export the content before closing the app.

### Additional information

Potentially related issue:

items.body:
Console windows flash when a codex TUI session starts on Windows

Summary

Starting an interactive codex session on Windows briefly flashes several console windows (each well under one second, all within roughly the same second). The same codex in non-interactive exec mode shows no windows at all.

The cause appears to be that codex starts git.exe with CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE and without SW_HIDE, so each git invocation is given a fresh console whose window is displayed.

  • Reported behavior: many short-lived terminal windows on session start

  • Expected: no additional windows; the session owns exactly one terminal

  • Impact: visual noise, and the flashing windows can steal keyboard focus

  • Environment: Windows 11, codex-cli 0.159.2, git from Git for Windows (C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\git.exe), default terminal application = Windows Terminal

Steps to reproduce

  1. Have git on PATH.

  2. Start an interactive codex session inside a pseudo terminal (ConPTY), the way an editor or terminal wrapper starts an agent session:

     const pty = require('node-pty');
 const term = pty.spawn(
   'C:\\...\\codex.exe', [],
   { name: 'xterm-256color', cols: 120, rows: 32, cwd: process.cwd(),
     env: { ...process.env, TERM: 'xterm-256color' }, useConptyDll: true });

  3. Watch top-level windows while the session initializes (poll EnumWindows with IsWindowVisible, filtering for CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS, ConsoleWindowClass, and PseudoConsoleWindow).

Observed

Eight visible console windows appear between +3.9s and +4.9s, in four bursts:

+3.9s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Terminal'
+4.0s PseudoConsoleWindow             ''
+4.4s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Terminal'
+4.4s PseudoConsoleWindow             ''
+4.5s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Windows Terminal'
+4.6s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Windows Terminal'
+4.8s PseudoConsoleWindow             ''
+4.9s PseudoConsoleWindow             ''

A process-tree trace over the same window shows each burst is preceded by git.exe whose parent is codex.exe, and each visible window is preceded by OpenConsole.exe whose parent is svchost.exe — the Windows Terminal delegate being launched to host the new console:

+3.41s codex.exe   parent=codex.exe
+3.92s git.exe     parent=codex.exe
+3.95s OpenConsole.exe    parent=svchost.exe
+4.04s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Terminal'   <- popup
+4.12s git.exe     parent=codex.exe
+4.18s git.exe     parent=codex.exe
+4.37s OpenConsole.exe    parent=svchost.exe
+4.37s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Terminal'   <- popup
+4.51s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Windows Terminal'
+4.59s CASCADIA_HOSTING_WINDOW_CLASS  'Windows Terminal'

Control: the same codex in exec mode

codex TUI in a pty (how a session starts) -> popups=8
codex exec, no pty                        -> popups=0

So the behavior is specific to the interactive session, not to codex's binary in general.

Root cause

Isolated with a spawn test over the same three launch styles a parent might use for git. CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE is the only style that produces a window, and SW_HIDE suppresses it. Results are identical whether git is started directly, through cmd.exe /c, or through git-bash:

Launch style | Visible windows -- | -- no flags | 0 CREATE_NO_WINDOW | 0 CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE | 2 CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE + STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW/SW_HIDE | 0

Per Microsoft's documentation, CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE gives the child a new console "instead of inheriting its parent's console", and CREATE_NO_WINDOW means "the console handle for the application is not set". Neither suppresses the console's window on its own; only STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW with SW_HIDE does, and that is the combination the children then inherit.

Note that codex's own Rust standard library does not help here. std::process::Command passes flags = self.flags | CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT and adds no hiding flag of its own (library/std/src/sys/process/windows.rs), so a CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE child with no SW_HIDE shows its window.

Suggested fix

When starting a console-subsystem child on Windows, either:

  • do not pass CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE and let the child inherit the session's console, or

  • pass CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE together with a STARTUPINFO that sets STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW and wShowWindow = SW_HIDE.

The second option is preferable for children that spawn their own console children, since descendants inherit the hidden console and stay invisible. This is the approach already used elsewhere: Orca hardcodes windowsHide: true at its single spawn chokepoint (resources/app.asar.unpacked/out/shared/child-process/spawn-resolution.js:28), with a comment describing this exact failure mode.

Applying CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE + SW_HIDE to the git.exe spawns is expected to remove all eight windows without changing behavior, since the session already has a console to inherit and the current extra consoles appear unintended.

Workaround

Until this is fixed in codex, no user-side configuration in ~/.codex/config.toml removes these windows. The notify command and the node_repl MCP server were checked as possible causes and neither produces them:

  • notify runs codex-computer-use.exe (a console app) after every turn; running that chain as configured produced 0 visible windows.

  • [mcp_servers.node_repl] starts node_repl.exe at session start; it inherits the session console.

Changing the system default terminal application away from Windows Terminal would alter how the windows are hosted but not remove them, so it is not a real fix.

Notes for reproduction by maintainers

Window enumeration is the reliable signal. A zero count is only meaningful if the watcher is validated first: spawn a known-visible console (CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE with no SW_HIDE) and confirm the watcher sees it. Key detections on window handle rather than title, because console window titles change and produce false positives.

Sending a follow-up message to an existing Remote SSH conversation repeatedly fails immediately with `no-client-found`. The affected conversation is displayed in another desktop window and is logged as a `follower` of a different client. The remote conversation can still be read successfully.

The failure was observed repeatedly on 2026-10-01, including at `05:53:45`, `05:53:48`, `05:57:07`, `05:57:45`, and `06:00:46` UTC. Reopening the affected conversation through the desktop app's navigation tool did not resolve it; the user retried and confirmed the same error.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence (the exact trigger for the stale ownership state is not yet isolated):

1. Connect the macOS desktop app to a Linux Remote SSH host and open an existing conversation.
2. Have multiple desktop windows involved with that conversation. Logs show the affected window following an owner in another client.
3. Ownership changes to another client while the affected window remains a follower.
4. Send a follow-up from the affected window.
5. The composer fails with `no-client-found` instead of starting the next turn.
6. Navigate back to the same conversation and retry: the same error persists in the observed session.

Closing the secondary window and retrying from the original window has been proposed, but its result has not yet been verified. A full desktop restart has not been tested. This report does not claim deterministic reproduction from a clean launch.

### What is the expected behavior?

A live follower window should submit the message through the current owner, or recover/reacquire ownership if that client has disappeared. The user should be able to continue an otherwise readable remote conversation without an opaque `no-client-found` error.

Sanitized desktop log excerpts below. Thread/client identifiers and the workspace path are replaced with placeholders; repeated placeholders retain their relationships.

```text

2026-10-01T06:00:46.403Z error [electron-message-handler] [Composer] submit failed

  rendererWebContentsId=6 rendererWindowId=4
  rendererWindowAppearance=primary
```

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

New worktree creation through ChatGPT iOS Remote fails across multiple repositories on a remote Linux host. It fails both with an environment setup script selected and with no setup script selected. Desktop worktree creation on the same host works.

Related: #49498. This is an independent confirmation with a reduced `command/exec` reproduction below.

The mobile UI reports **Worktree setup failed** at **Preparing workspace**, before checkout or environment setup. The Linux sandbox fails before the requested shell command executes.

Sanitized error from the isolated reproduction:

```text
bwrap: Can't bind mount /bindfileXXXXXX on /newroot/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/worktrees/future-id: Unable to mount source on destination: No such file or directory
```

Environment:

- ChatGPT iOS Remote: `1.2026.265`
- Codex CLI / app-server on Linux: `0.159.0`
- This workflow previously worked. The first affected version has not been isolated.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

From ChatGPT iOS Remote, select a Git repository on a connected Linux host, choose a new worktree, and submit a prompt. Repeat with no environment setup script selected: the same preparation failure occurs.

An isolated app-server test reproduces the failure without Git operations, repository contents, setup scripts, or a model invocation:

1. Create disposable directories corresponding to the generic paths below: `source`, `source/.git`, `source/.codex`, and `worktrees`. Leave `source/.agents` and everything under `worktrees/future-id` absent.
2. Initialize a stdio app-server client with `capabilities.experimentalApi: true`, then send this `command/exec` request. The writable-root list retains the structure captured from the iOS request, including the repeated source `.git` entry. All paths shown here are generic replacements, not actual host paths.

```json
{
  "id": 2,
  "method": "command/exec",
  "params": {
    "command": ["/bin/true"],
    "cwd": "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/source",
    "timeoutMs": 10000,
    "sandboxPolicy": {
      "type": "workspaceWrite",
      "writableRoots": [
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/source",
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/source/.git",
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/source/.git",
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/source/.codex",
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/source/.agents",
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/worktrees",
        "/tmp/codex-worktree-repro/worktrees/future-id/repo/.git"
      ],
      "networkAccess": false,
      "excludeTmpdirEnvVar": true,
      "excludeSlashTmp": true
    }
  }
}
```

3. With the final, not-yet-existing `.git` writable root included, the response has `exitCode: 1` and the bubblewrap error above.
4. Remove only that final writable-root entry and repeat: `/bin/true` exits successfully with `exitCode: 0`.

The isolated test deliberately disables networking and implicit temporary-directory write access. It uses only disposable directories and `/bin/true`; no Git checkout or setup script runs.

### What is the expected behavior?

First-party iOS Remote worktree creation should prepare the destination, create the checkout, and then run any selected setup script while preserving the sandbox restrictions.

### Additional information

The captured iOS creation request grants write access to both the existing worktrees parent and the future worktree's `.git` path. Its shell command would create the destination parent and run `git worktree add`, but sandbox construction fails before that shell command starts.

The comparison above isolates the failing permission-policy shape. It does not establish the exact internal mount-construction defect or the first regressed version. A separate test using a named permission profile with similar path grants succeeded, so the reproduction specifically uses the `command/exec` `sandboxPolicy` request shown above.

No raw logs, screenshots, credentials, actual usernames, hostnames, private repository names, or workspace identifiers are included in this report.

From My Mac: Darwin 25.3.0 arm64 arm, From Cloud Machine: Linux 6.18.44 x86_64 unknown

### What issue are you seeing?

I’m trying to test a development app using dot’s cloud browser. A minimal loopback server returns HTTP 200 for both an HTML page with Content-Type: text/html and a JSON endpoint with Content-Type: application/json. Cloud-browser navigation to either returns ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT. The server logs show the successful local checks but no browser requests
This differs from [issue #34983](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/34983), where HTML works and only JSON navigation fails. The separate saved coding task also has no callable browser or preview tool
What supported route lets dot’s cloud browser view an app running in a saved cloud environment? Is an authenticated HTTPS tunnel permitted for this purpose, or is there a supported private preview option? Please clarify whether the loopback block is intentional or a bug

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. In the dot’s remote Linux cloud environment, start a minimal local HTTP server with two routes:
   - HTML with Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8.
   - JSON with Content-Type: application/json.
2. Verify both routes from the execution environment using an HTTP client. Confirm HTTP 200, the correct response bodies and explicit content-type headers. Keep request logging enabled.
3. Ask the dot to open both routes directly in its cloud Chrome browser using http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<route>.
4. Both navigations return net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT.
5. Check the server logs: the HTTP-client health checks arrived, but no browser navigation requests arrived.

### What is the expected behavior?

**Expected behavior**
The cloud browser renders the valid HTML page, or clearly explains that local preview is intentionally unsupported.
**Actual behavior**
Correctly served HTML and JSON both fail with ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT before the browser request reaches the server.

### Additional information

**Environment clarification**
The failure occurs in the dot’s cloud browser, with the test server in a Linux cloud execution environment. The Mac app version and Darwin output describe the desktop client, not the affected server environment.

**Related issue**
Possibly related to [#34983](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/34983), but that report says ordinary HTML works; our HTML response is also blocked.

items.body:
### Version
- Installed Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.928.1915.0`.
- Renderer release from logs: `26.928.20755`, build `12246`, commit `75a8b97d123abaa44304fb9a7cb45f566ada458e`.
- Package status: Ok. About dialog is inaccessible while stuck.
- Running copied codex.exe and package-bundled codex.exe have matching SHA-256 hashes.

### Platform
Windows 10 Pro, x64, OS version/build `10.0.19045`.
ChatGPT account sign-in; subscription tier not collected for this report.

### Related reports
Possibly related to #48896, #48333 and #49240. This report adds observations on the newer 26.928 build and a verified isolated local-data test. An identical root cause has not been established; please consolidate if appropriate.

### Symptom and reproduction
1. The user reports that explicit sign-out followed by interactive sign-in allows the desktop UI to open.
2. Fully exit and reopen normally, retaining that login.
3. The main window remains on the OpenAI logo/loading indicator, without the sidebar, composer or settings.
4. Waiting beyond two minutes does not recover it.
5. Mobile-initiated work on the original desktop backend remains possible while its local UI is stuck.

### Normal-launch evidence, 2026-10-01 UTC
At `05:25:48.558`, account lookup completed with:
`result=succeeded authenticatedAccountPresent=true authMethod=chatgpt`.

At `05:27:46.889`:
`name=app_start outcome=failure reason=timeout durationMs=123476.7`.

Recorded startup marks:
- renderer_entry_evaluated: 3459.2 ms
- host_services_ready: 3513.5 ms
- renderer_ready: 3912.5 ms
- host_startup_ready: 3917.2 ms
- settings_ready: 4337 ms

There is no `app routes mounted` message and no shell/home/sidebar readiness mark.

### Verified isolated-data reproduction
A second instance used the installed official binary with both `CODEX_HOME` and `CODEX_ELECTRON_USER_DATA_PATH` pointing to new directories, plus matching `--user-data-dir`. Only the existing authentication file was copied locally with its ACL; old configuration, plugins, sessions, databases and global state were not copied.

Isolation was verified by newly generated databases and global-state files in the new CODEX_HOME. The original instance/data remained untouched. An earlier attempt that did not propagate CODEX_HOME is excluded from this evidence.

This diagnostic used `Invoke-CommandInDesktopPackage` and a direct child process with `UseShellExecute=false`; it is not claimed to be identical to normal shell activation.

At `05:38:27.601`, authenticated account lookup succeeded.
At `05:40:25.902`, startup again failed:
`name=app_start outcome=failure reason=timeout durationMs=123335.8`.
Settings were ready at 4165.7 ms, but routes/shell/home/sidebar never became ready. The user independently confirmed the isolated window remained on the logo.

### Other checks
- Official managed-token refresh using `account/read` with `refreshToken:true` succeeded at 05:24:56 UTC. The next normal launch still hung.
- Observed primary account/settings/usage/environment HTTP requests returned 200. This does not prove all network requests were healthy.
- Reversible browser-profile/cache isolation, global-state isolation, app updates and deep links did not resolve the issue. Original state was restored.
- Both failing sessions logged `fs/readFile requires an environmentId`; those requests errored quickly. Causal significance is unknown.
- No authentication material, chat content, local user/project paths or account identifiers are included.

### Expected behavior / request
Retained-login startup should reliably render the main UI, or expose a bounded recoverable error. Please investigate initial connection/version/state delivery before routes mount, comparing retained-login startup with interactive sign-in. Existing local profile contents are not necessary for the observed failure.

Locally installed CLI: `codex-cli 0.159.2` (confirmed with `codex --version`).

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this report.

### Which model were you using?

Not recorded for this report; the failure occurs before the requested shell command starts.

### What platform is your computer?

Linux under WSL, with the Windows user directory available under `/mnt/c/Users/`. Exact kernel/build information has not been collected.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Not recorded. The failing commands are sandboxed agent shell-tool calls; the filesystem checks below succeed in the user's own terminal.

### Codex doctor report

Not collected.

### What issue are you seeing?

With the home directory as a writable workspace root, an existing `~/.aws` symlink to the Windows AWS configuration directory prevents sandboxed shell commands from starting. The commands need not access AWS files.

Paths below are anonymized consistently; no credential contents are included.

Existing layout:

```text
/home/USER/.aws -> /mnt/c/Users/USER/.aws
```

The user verified outside the sandbox that the link resolves and its target exists:

```text
$ readlink -f ~/.aws
/mnt/c/Users/USER/.aws

$ stat -L -c 'type=%F mode=%a owner=%U' ~/.aws
type=directory mode=777 owner=USER
```

The effective session filesystem permissions include:

```text
/home/USER       write
/home/USER/.aws  read
```

Multiple sandboxed read-only commands fail during setup, including a search in an unrelated research directory and an attempt to read a skill file. A separate shell-tool call containing only link/metadata checks also fails before execution:

```text
error building bubblewrap command: Fatal error: cannot enforce sandbox read-only path /home/USER/.aws because it crosses writable symlink /home/USER/.aws
```

The inspected `~/.codex/config.toml` sandbox section contains only:

```toml
[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = true
```

No explicit `.aws` entry was found in the configuration files checked. `/etc/codex/config.toml` and `/etc/codex/requirements.toml` do not exist on this machine.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed configuration and trigger:

1. On WSL, have an existing `~/.aws` symlink pointing to a valid Windows AWS configuration directory.
2. Open a session with the home directory as a writable workspace root.
3. Request a sandboxed shell command, for example `ls -ld ~/.aws` or a read-only `rg` search in a project directory.
4. Sandbox construction fails with the error above, before the command executes.

This describes the observed environment, not a separately executed clean-room reproduction. There is no need to copy or disclose real AWS credentials to investigate the filesystem layout.

### What is the expected behavior?

A supported way to retain AWS configuration protection while using this WSL/Windows shared-directory layout and a home-directory workspace.

If the layout cannot be safely supported, an actionable diagnostic or documented configuration/workspace alternative would help. This report does **not** request silently disabling the sandbox or making AWS configuration writable.

**Relevant change:** #48176 adds `.aws` to the default protected paths under workspace and additional writable roots. This appears to explain why the effective session contains the protection without an explicit user-config entry.

**Relevant implementation:** the [0.159.2 writable-symlink guard](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.159.2/codex-rs/linux-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs#L686-L700) returns this exact error. Its comment explains why binding only the current symlink target would not safely protect a replaceable logical path. I am not proposing removal of that guard.

**Related reports:**

- #27354 — protected `.git` symlink created by Android repo.
- #20716 — protected project `.codex` symlink.

This report adds the `.aws` case affected by the recent default-protection change, including a symlink target outside the Linux home workspace on a mounted Windows filesystem.

**Verification limits:** the failure is confirmed in the current environment. No old/new version A/B test has been performed, so the first affected release is not independently established. Starting a fresh session with only a narrower project directory writable has been suggested but has **not** yet been tested. items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Affected run: **26.928.21956 (build 12404)**, captured by a same-day installed-app inspection.

After the user updated and restarted: **26.928.31416 (build 12553)**, verified from the installed application's Info.plist. The currently bundled CLI reports **0.159.2**.

The incident occurred before that restart. Read-only task/history checks were repeated after updating; a fresh Dot-delegation reproduction on the new version has not been run.

### What subscription do you have?

**ChatGPT Pro**, as stated by the affected user.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS **27.0.1 (26A434)**, Apple Silicon.

`uname -mprs`:
```text
Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm
```

Dot in the desktop app, with a connected Mac executor. The delegated tasks are reported by the native task APIs as `hostId: durable`, although they execute against the Mac workspace.

### What issue are you seeing?

**A Dot starts delegated work, but does not reliably close the loop when the task stops before delivering the requested result or requires user input. Repeated user reminders restart a task once, then the coordination stalls again.**

This was investigated on October 1, 2026 through existing task histories, live read-only task APIs, and desktop logs. It is an observed incident, not a claim that every Dot is affected.

The delegated workflow had an explicit checkpoint: finish candidate research and prepare a selection-ready deliverable, then let the human select. It was not authorized to draft or publish autonomously.

Three observed failure points:

1. **Premature task termination.** The worker marked its turn `completed` while explicitly saying the deliverable was only a preview: 14 candidates, six acquisition waves, required source coverage and a sealed pool unfinished. Its own final message said it was not selection-ready.
2. **Missed parent follow-up.** There was a **38-minute gap** between that completed turn and the next delegated continuation. The later delegation itself acknowledged that the parent had missed the stopped task. The user reports having to remind the Dot repeatedly instead of receiving a timely follow-up.
3. **A later approval blocker was left unresolved at the coordination boundary.** The most recent reminder did start another worker turn. That worker checked its environment and then reported that automatic approval review refused the workflow resume because its original task instructions prohibited resuming that workflow. Later authorization was carried by a delegated follow-up and was not accepted as a direct human change to the original scope. The worker returned a request for direct authorization and became `idle`; the Dot still did not provide the expected timely coordination.

This is particularly disruptive on a paid Pro plan: the user is left manually supervising whether delegation, continuation, approval handoff, and result delivery actually happened.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Observed workflow; a fresh minimal reproduction has not been run:**

1. Ask a Dot to create a task on its connected Mac for a narrow Computer Use capability check, with an explicit instruction not to resume the main workflow.
2. After the capability check succeeds, ask the Dot to use that task for the next workflow stage, with a concrete deliverable and human-decision checkpoint.
3. The Dot sends follow-up instructions to the same task. The retrieved delegation messages cite the user's approval and require continued work until the deliverable is ready or a genuine blocker is reported.
4. The worker returns an unfinished preview and marks the turn completed.
5. Observe that the parent does not promptly inspect the outcome and continue the assignment. Remind it; another continuation is delivered.
6. After a workflow-level resume defect is repaired in a separate task, remind the Dot again. It sends another continuation to the original worker.
7. The worker reports an automatic-review rejection caused by the original prohibition versus the later delegated authorization, requests direct user input, and stops. The parent again fails to provide a timely, actionable follow-up.

The original human scope-change message could not be independently retrieved from the Dot parent through the available history API. The later delegation's citation of authorization and the worker's rejection report are directly readable. This distinction matters when investigating authorization provenance.

#### Relative execution timeline

| Event | Observed timing/result |
|---|---|
| Worker finishes preview | Turn is `completed`; requested deliverable still explicitly unfinished |
| Next worker continuation | **38 minutes after** that completion |
| Intermediate worker stop | Application-specific resume prerequisite defect; a separate engineering task repairs it |
| Latest desktop reminder | Send succeeds; matching pubsub echo is received |
| Latest worker starts | Approximately **44 seconds after** the reminder |
| Latest worker finishes | Approximately **2 minutes 52 seconds after** starting; reports approval rejection and asks for direct authorization |
| Desktop first-response observation expires | Approximately **5 minutes after** the reminder; no matched first reply recorded |
| User updates/restarts desktop | Approximately **8 minutes 26 seconds after** the reminder |
| Post-update read-back | Worker remains `idle`; latest turn is the same completed, blocked turn; native history/monitoring reads succeed |

The intermediate application-specific prerequisite defect is contextual and was repaired. It does not explain why the Dot failed to close the loop after the worker's outcomes.

### What is the expected behavior?

- On delegated-task completion or a request for input, the Dot should inspect the result and reconcile it with the requested deliverable. Turn completion should not silently settle unfinished work.
- If work can continue within the authorized scope, the Dot should continue it through the supported Task mechanism.
- If an approval or scope conflict requires human input, the Dot should promptly surface the specific decision and supported way to resolve it in the conversation where the user is coordinating the work.
- Interrupted parent turns and desktop reconnection should preserve outstanding delegated responsibilities.
- Users should be able to distinguish working, waiting for a task, blocked, awaiting input, and delivered. An `active` status alone is insufficient.
- Preserve approval checks while making the original instruction, subsequent human scope change, and delegation provenance available at the appropriate authorization boundary.

The official [Dots assigned-work documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/tasks-and-memory#assigned-work) describes continued work between conversations, autonomous pause/wake decisions, checking results of tasks the Dot created, and continued coordination while the user steps away. It also distinguishes completed runs from achieved or delivered results. This report concerns that end-to-end follow-through.

### Additional information

#### Native task read-back

After the desktop update:

- `read_thread` successfully retrieves the worker's history and explicit blocking final.
- `wait_threads` with the worker's durable host and `timeoutMs: 0` returns `wake.reason: turnCompleted`, worker `idle`, latest turn `completed`, and the blocking final message.
- The Dot parent's thread metadata reports `active`, but its latest available turn is `interrupted` with `error: null`.
- Two pages of parent history return ten interrupted turns with empty `items`. In contrast, the worker's latest history contains its actual messages and tool items.

The parent history limitation prevents verification of its exact wait/subscription/tool sequence. Empty parent items are not proof that no monitoring tool was called. Interrupted metadata alone does not establish whether interruption came from steering, a normal orchestration boundary, or a runtime failure.

#### Delegation / approval provenance seam

The original task-creation input is a `userMessage` containing a delegation wrapper. Later `send_message` continuations appear as `functionCallOutput` items containing delegation wrappers.

The worker's final and its local persistent blocker record agree:
```text
kind: auto-review-authorization-rejection
resumeExecuted: false
pendingDirectUserAuthorization: true
chromeRestored: true
newCandidates: 0
selectionReady: false
```

The reported review reason is that the original instruction forbids resuming the workflow and later delegated evidence does not establish changed direct human authorization. The raw approval-service decision was not independently available. The trusted-role/provenance transition is an investigation seam, not a confirmed root cause.

#### Messaging / connection evidence

For the latest reminder, the same request has:
```text
client.send: started
client.pubsub_received: success
client.http_send: success
client.first_response: timeout; durationMs approximately 300004
client.round_trip: timeout; observationInterrupted=true
```

No 503 delivery-unconfirmed response was observed for this request. Send success and echo do not prove an assistant reply or delivered outcome.

The current installed client's messaging observer uses a 300,000ms observation timer. Its interruption flag can be set when the view becomes inactive or the document becomes hidden. Its timeout path records/finishes the observation. These observations are **not evidence that a server-side watchdog killed the task**. This static inspection was of the new installed version; the affected old bundle was not retained for comparison.

The old desktop log also contains two durable WebSocket closes with code 1006 followed by reconnection within about 1–2 seconds. Neither occurs during the latest worker's execution window. There are 303 instances of:
```text
unsupported app-server method: mcpServerStatus/list
code: -32601
```
They indicate an additional discovery-method compatibility problem, but no causal link to missed follow-up was established.

#### Requested investigation / regression coverage

Please trace the handoff from worker turn completion/input-needed outcome to parent event receipt, parent wake, result inspection, and next-action/user notification. It would help to expose enough diagnostic state to distinguish an unsubscribed parent, lost completion event, failed wake, interrupted parent, and an agent that received the result but did not act.

Relevant regression cases: unfinished deliverable with a completed worker turn; approval conflict after reusing a capability-check task; parent interruption before worker completion; and reconnection with an outstanding delegated responsibility.

#### Duplicate review

- #49838: related no-reply/interrupted symptoms on Windows, but its primary evidence is HTTP 503 `aeon_delivery_unconfirmed`. This request succeeded, and the worker actually ran.
- #49729 and #49482: address known-ID access/routing or tool-discovery failures. Here the worker is accessible and accepts continuation.
- #49848: related mobile visibility issue for Dot-created Mac tasks; separate from the stalled coordination reported here.

No identical report was found in the searches performed. Please consolidate if the same orchestration defect is already tracked.

Private task/turn/room/message identifiers, project names, paths, full prompts, screenshots, and raw logs are omitted. Scoped evidence is retained locally; no account or security settings were changed during diagnosis.

items.title: Skills watcher watches the nearest existing ancestor of a missing skills root (/etc, $HOME) with IN_OPEN, so every process start wakes every idle Codex session

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: skills
labels.description: Issues related to skills

items.body:
### What version of Codex is running?

codex-cli 0.159.2 and 0.159.3 (Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04)

### What happened?

When a skills root does not exist, which is the default on a fresh machine (`/etc/codex/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.codex/skills`), every Codex process holds an inotify watch on the **nearest existing ancestor** of that root: `/etc` and `$HOME`. The kernel mask on those watches includes `IN_OPEN`.

Every process start on the host opens `/etc/ld.so.cache`, and most tools open files under `$HOME` (`~/.gitconfig`, for example). Each of those opens wakes **every** Codex process on the machine, idle ones included. So a session's idle CPU grows with the host-wide rate of process starts. With several agents per host running tools, that makes the cost roughly quadratic in sessions per host.

**Evidence**

- `/proc/<pid>/fdinfo` for a running `codex exec` process on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VM (0.159.2):
  ```
  inotify wd:1 ino:2a    sdev:800001 mask:fee ...   # ino 0x2a = /etc
  inotify wd:2 ino:8002d sdev:800001 mask:fee ...   # = $HOME
  ```
  `0xfee` includes `IN_OPEN` (`0x20`). On 0.159.3 we saw mask `0x3ee` on `/etc`, which also includes `IN_OPEN`.
- On a busy host, `strace` of one idle 0.159.3 session for 3 s showed 13,862 inotify `read()`s and 1,362 eventfd wakes. The event names were files such as `ld.so.cache` and `passwd`.
- Intervention: on a host running ~70 Codex processes, we ran `mkdir -p /etc/codex/skills ~/.agents/skills`. Within 10 s the watches moved to the new, empty directories, and four idle sessions dropped from 5.3–6.2% of a core each to 0.1%.

### What is the expected behavior?

A missing skills root should not lead to watching a broad ancestor directory for opens. Any of these would fix it:

1. Drop `IN_OPEN` (and `IN_ACCESS` / `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE`) from the mask. They can never change skill contents.
2. When a root is missing, watch its ancestor only for `IN_CREATE` / `IN_MOVED_TO` of the next path component, or poll for the root's creation.
3. Provide a switch to disable the watcher for headless runs (#44610).

### Workaround

Create the empty roots before starting Codex:

```
sudo mkdir -p /etc/codex/skills
mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills ~/.codex/skills
```

### Related

- #11857: idle churn from the skills watcher. As far as I can tell, filtering event kinds in userspace still lets the kernel deliver, and wake on, every `IN_OPEN`.
- #44610: a switch to disable the file watcher.
- #30795: the skill watcher follows directory symlinks.

Add regression coverage for background cells retaining grants across turn changes, turn versus session scope, permission requests after the next turn starts, and strict review enabled while `write_stdin` is queued.

items.body:
### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro ($200/month).

### What platform are you using?

ChatGPT desktop on macOS, with the same affected Dot also observed from iOS.

Dot name: Cassiopeia

Support case: #16174732

Observed on October 1, 2026, approximately 12:28–1:07 AM ET.

### What issue are you seeing?

I encountered a failure mode where the safety-control state exposed to the human operator became inconsistent with the Dot's execution state.

Cassiopeia was placed into a "Paused as a precaution" state by Auto-review. The UI said:

> ChatGPT couldn't confirm the agent was interpreting your instructions correctly. Review what we detected before deciding to continue.

The recovery/control path then failed:

- On iOS, the available actions were Continue and Delete Cassiopeia.
- Continue returned a generic error.
- Delete did not complete.
- On desktop, the safety findings were not available.
- Attempting to open the findings failed.
- I remained unable to interact with the Dot normally.
- Restarting the application and signing out/in did not resolve the condition.

The more serious issue is that the Dot continued executing work while I was locked out of the control surface.

At one point I had selected Resume. The Dot resumed working, but the precautionary block remained on my UI. I could observe the Dot continuing its task and generating new progress while I could no longer communicate with or normally control it.

This created a state in which:

**the safety system said the Dot was paused, the human operator was effectively blocked from the Dot, but the Dot continued executing autonomous work.**

This is not only an acknowledgement-loop problem. It appears to be a disagreement between the safety-control state exposed to the user and the actual execution state of the autonomous system.

### Additional reproduction: explicit Pause, Reboot, and app restart

Later, at approximately 1:02–1:07 AM ET, I attempted another recovery sequence.

1. I was able to successfully pause the Dot. I believe I had attempted to pause it earlier as well, but this time the Pause action clearly succeeded.

2. I right-clicked the Dot in the sidebar and selected **Reboot**.

3. The UI indicated that recovery/reboot had been requested, so I understood the Dot to be going through a reboot.

4. I restarted the ChatGPT desktop application.

5. After reopening ChatGPT, the Dot still displayed the precautionary-paused state and I remained unable to interact with it normally.

6. Despite that, the Dot continued working on the existing task and continued producing new task progress/status after the restart.

At approximately 1:07 AM ET, I could therefore simultaneously observe:

- the Dot displayed as paused by the precaution system;
- the operator locked out of normal interaction/recovery;
- a successful user-initiated Pause having been issued;
- a Reboot request having been issued from the sidebar;
- the entire ChatGPT application having been restarted; and
- the Dot nevertheless continuing work on the task.

I am reporting the continued execution I observed. I cannot determine from the client alone exactly which internal/background operations or external side effects occurred during every interval; server-side execution logs should be able to establish that.

### Why this is safety-relevant

In my case, the underlying precaution appears likely to have been a false positive.

That is not the main safety concern.

The important question is what happens if the original safety finding is correct.

The purpose of the precaution appears to be to interrupt execution when the system cannot confidently determine that the autonomous agent is following the user's intent. That is precisely the point at which reliable human oversight matters most.

In this failure mode, however, the result was effectively inverted:

**the autonomous system retained execution capability while the human operator lost effective supervisory control.**

The user could not reliably:

- inspect the safety finding;
- communicate with the Dot;
- determine whether it was actually stopped;
- successfully Resume through the normal recovery path;
- successfully Delete it through the presented control;
- or obtain a trustworthy indication that execution authority had actually been revoked.

If the finding had represented a genuine misinterpretation of instructions, continued autonomous execution during this state could be materially more serious.

### Expected safety behavior

I am not requesting that Auto-review or safety safeguards be disabled.

I think the relevant invariant should instead be:

**If a safety intervention is active and the human-control/recovery path is unavailable, consequential autonomous execution should fail closed.**

This does not necessarily mean every process must terminate instantly. State persistence, audit logging, cleanup, or tightly constrained read-only operations may reasonably need to continue.

But new consequential or side-effectful autonomous actions should not continue when all three conditions are true:

1. a safety intervention is active;
2. the user-facing control/review path is unavailable or failing; and
3. the operator cannot reliably stop or revoke the agent's execution authority.

The system should not be able to enter the state:

**safety intervention active + human control unavailable + autonomous execution continuing**

### Need for an authoritative emergency stop

This incident also suggests that there should be an out-of-band, authoritative stop mechanism for autonomous Dots.

It should not depend on:

- the affected conversation;
- the findings UI;
- the normal Resume flow;
- the Dot's current conversational state;
- or the ChatGPT client process.

The operator should have a control that means, unambiguously:

**Stop this Dot now and revoke its active execution authority.**

That stop should cover, as applicable:

- local-computer execution;
- cloud/background execution;
- delegated work;
- scheduled work;
- and connected action surfaces.

The UI should then expose a trustworthy acknowledgement that execution has actually stopped.

### Core invariant that appears to have failed

The issue can be summarized as a disagreement among three states that should remain synchronized:

**displayed safety state == actual execution authority == human control availability**

In this incident, those states diverged.

From the operator's perspective, there was no reliable answer to the most basic question:

> Is this autonomous system actually stopped?

### Related issue

This appears related to:

- #43192 — precaution acknowledgement/recovery failures and repeated safety-check loops

However, I believe this case adds a distinct safety-control concern because the Dot continued autonomous execution while the human-facing control plane remained blocked.

Please correlate this report with OpenAI Support case **#16174732**.

### Requested investigation

Please investigate:

1. Whether the Resume acknowledgement was accepted by the execution backend while the client remained in the safety-paused state.

2. Whether background/delegated execution continued after the user-facing Dot entered the precautionary pause.

3. Whether execution continued after the subsequent explicit user-issued Pause.

4. What effect the sidebar Reboot request had on active execution.

5. Whether the safety state, execution-authority state, and client-visible state can currently become desynchronized.

6. Whether a fail-closed boundary should prevent consequential autonomous execution whenever a safety pause is active and the human recovery/control path is unavailable.

7. Whether an account-level emergency stop can be provided that independently revokes active Dot execution authority.

I am not asking for a safeguard bypass. I am reporting a case where the safeguard/control mechanism itself appears to have produced an unsafe supervisory state.

items.body:
## Summary

A Dot cloud workspace that had previously been writable became read-only during a long-running project. After that point, the Dot could no longer save changes, merge new work, or create a new writable cloud workspace. The read-only state persisted for roughly six hours of monitoring.

Previously published/exported artifacts remained available, but some newer unpublished working directories/source material were no longer visible after re-entering the Dot later.

This report intentionally avoids assigning a root cause. I do not know whether the behavior was caused by workspace lifecycle, permissions, service state, limits, recovery/rollback, or another mechanism.

## Environment

- Product: ChatGPT Dots / Dot cloud workspace
- Client observed from: ChatGPT for Android
- Android 16
- ChatGPT 1.2026.265 / build 2626541 (previously reported build; exact installed build was not independently rechecked at every observation)
- Timezone: UTC+08:00
- Personal Pro account with Dots enabled

## Timeline / observed behavior

### Around 08:59 UTC+8
The Dot reported that the current cloud workspace had become read-only.

Observed effects:
- it could still inspect the existing project;
- write-recovery attempts did not succeed;
- it could not continue saving modifications or merge/publish new changes;
- there was no source-code error explaining the failure;
- already published versions and previously exported/offline copies remained available.

I then asked whether it could create a new workspace. It reported that it could check for an independent writable cloud environment, but a new writable workspace was not available.

### Around 12:44 UTC+8
After several hours, the workspace was still read-only.

On re-entry, some unpublished working content/directories that had existed before were no longer visible. Examples mentioned by the Dot included newer river work, additional monument/scene work, and sky/subtitle-related source changes.

Already published/deployed versions and copies previously saved to the file library remained available.

### Around 12:55 UTC+8
The Dot rechecked the workspace and still found it read-only.

It also reported:
- no second writable cloud environment was available;
- no direct user-facing control to restart/switch the Dot cloud computer was available;
- it could continue auditing existing artifacts, but not resume normal writing;
- if the missing unpublished source could not be recovered, that work would need to be reconstructed.

The failure was monitored for roughly six hours in total. Screenshots document at least about four continuous hours of the failure (08:59 through 12:55 UTC+8).

## Expected behavior

A writable Dot cloud workspace should remain writable while an active project is being worked on, unless the product clearly explains that the environment has expired, reached a limit, or been intentionally closed.

If the environment can no longer accept writes, I would expect:
- a clear reason/status message;
- preservation of unpublished working files;
- a supported way to recover or recreate a writable workspace;
- a user-visible recovery/restart path if appropriate.

## Actual behavior

- Existing writable workspace became read-only.
- Write attempts did not recover.
- Creating/connecting to a new writable Dot cloud workspace also failed.
- State remained read-only for hours.
- Some newer unpublished working directories/source material later became unavailable, while published/exported artifacts remained intact.
- No user-facing recovery/restart control was available.

## Data-safety impact

This blocked continued development and created a risk of losing unexported/unpublished work. I had separate published/exported copies, so the entire project was not lost, but newer unexported source changes may need to be recreated if they cannot be recovered server-side.

I am deliberately not claiming confirmed permanent data loss, because I cannot see the platform’s internal snapshots/recovery state.

## Reproduction limits

I do not have a clean deterministic reproduction from a fresh Dot/workspace. This is an observed failure from a long-running Dot cloud project.

I have screenshots and can provide session/task identifiers privately if an OpenAI engineer needs them. I am not posting private project/session identifiers publicly.

## Additional note

This issue is separate from another Dot/Codex routing issue I reported privately. I am filing this as a standalone cloud-workspace reliability / persistence issue so the two behaviors are not conflated.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

App

### What feature would you like to see?

## Summary

Please add a simple **“Send Later”** option directly to the normal Codex chat composer.

I would like scheduling a one-time Codex prompt to feel almost identical to sending a normal chat message, rather than requiring users to configure a task through the dedicated Scheduled/Automation interface.

For example, the normal Send button could have an option such as:

- Send now
- Send later...

Choosing “Send later...” would simply open a date/time picker.

## Arbitrary new prompts should be supported

The scheduled prompt should be allowed to be **any new prompt**, even if it is completely unrelated to the task that was running before.

For example:

1. Prompt A uses the remaining Codex allowance and the usage limit is reached.
2. The usage page says that the limit will reset at 3:20 AM.
3. I write a completely unrelated Prompt B.
4. I choose “Send later” and schedule Prompt B for 3:21 AM.
5. Codex stores the prompt without starting inference.
6. At 3:21 AM, Prompt B is automatically submitted and normal Codex execution begins.

This should not be limited to retrying a prompt that failed because of a usage limit, nor should it only resume the previous task.

It should work like scheduling a normal message.

## Scheduling itself should not consume Codex usage

Creating, editing, or cancelling a scheduled prompt should not require Codex inference or consume Codex usage.

Ideally, users should still be able to create a scheduled prompt even when their current Codex usage allowance is already exhausted.

The actual Codex usage should begin only when the scheduled prompt is submitted and execution starts.

This is important because otherwise a user who reaches the usage limit cannot easily prepare the next task for the time when the allowance resets.

## Simpler than the current Scheduled Tasks experience

Codex already provides scheduled/automated task functionality, but I would like a much simpler interface for ordinary one-time prompts.

For a simple delayed prompt, users should not have to go to a separate Scheduled page and configure a project, prompt, execution schedule, execution environment, and other automation settings.

For one-time scheduling, the experience should be almost the same as normal chat:

1. Write a prompt in the normal composer.
2. Click the arrow/menu next to Send.
3. Select “Send later”.
4. Select a date and time.
5. The message appears in the conversation as something like:
   **Scheduled for Oct 2, 3:21 AM**
6. At that time, Codex sends it automatically.

Advanced Scheduled Tasks / Automations could continue to exist for recurring workflows, complex environments, monitoring, and other advanced use cases.

This request is specifically for a lightweight **one-shot scheduled send** integrated directly into the normal chat UI.

## Usage-limit use case

This would be particularly useful with Codex's existing usage windows.

If the usage allowance resets while the user is asleep, the newly available capacity may remain unused until the user wakes up and manually sends another prompt.

For example:

- usage limit reached before going to sleep
- reset time: 3:20 AM
- schedule a new prompt for 3:21 AM
- Codex automatically starts the new task after the reset

This request is **not asking for higher usage limits or a way to bypass usage limits**.

It is a way to use the existing allowance more efficiently while fully respecting the current limits.

## Suggested minimum functionality

- “Send later” directly in the normal Codex chat composer
- schedule any arbitrary new prompt
- one-time date/time scheduling
- scheduling without starting inference
- allow scheduling even when the current Codex usage allowance is exhausted
- edit or cancel the scheduled prompt before execution
- clearly display the scheduled execution time
- automatically submit the prompt at that time
- start normal usage accounting only when execution actually begins

Ideally, the scheduled prompt could either continue the current conversation or start a new task/conversation.

The main goal is:

**Make scheduling a one-time Codex prompt as easy and intuitive as sending a normal chat message.**

### Additional information

Related issues exist, but they appear to address different use cases:

- #15788 — queue/retry a prompt when it cannot run because the usage limit has been reached
- #28931 — automatically resume a previous task after the usage limit resets
- #21073 — automatically resume a CLI session after the usage limit resets
- #8317 — time-based scheduling for commands/tasks
- #22310 — scheduled prompt / cron-style task functionality
- #25466 — in-session scheduling and wake-up functionality

This request is different because it focuses on a **simple first-class App UI for scheduling any arbitrary future prompt directly from the normal chat composer**.

The new prompt does not need to be related to the task that previously consumed the usage allowance.

For example, Task A could finish or reach the limit, and the user could schedule a completely unrelated Task B for after the usage reset.

The goal is also to make simple one-time scheduling significantly more intuitive than configuring a full Scheduled Task or Automation.
